To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
CD16(+)CD56(-) NK cells express high IFN-alphaR, and this is associated with the IFN-alpha-induced decline in HCV RNA.

the CD56(-)CD16(+) NK cells are the major producers of IFN-α in HCV patients, and that the expression of IFN-γ receptor (R) on NK cells regulates the signaling and is implicated with the IFN-α induced HCV RNA decline.
IFN-αR expression in CD16(+) 56(-) NK cells is genetically determined, and is associated with the magnitude of IFN-α induced HCV decline.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the CD16(+)CD56(-) NK cell population in the context of HCV infection.
the development of a mathematical model for the analysis of the effects of the treatment with IFN-α and PEG-IFN-α in chronic hepatitis C patients.
the role of natural killer cells and their cytokines in the immune response to hepatitis C virus infection and the development of the liver disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results of the present study suggest the existence of a genetic association of the CD16(+) CD56(−) natural killer (NK) cells with the IFN-αR expression and the IFN-γR expression in patients with hepatitis C.

the results of this study suggest that CD16(+) NK cells are the major source of IFN-α in the blood of HCV patients and that the CD56(+) subset of NK cells is the major source of this cytokine in PBMC.

the use of the term "natural killer cell" should be avoided, and that CD16(+)CD56(-) cells should be described as "CD16(+)CD3(-) cells", or "CD16(+/+) CD3(-) cells" if CD16(+) cells are being compared with CD16(-) cells.

The main takeaway from our work is that
we identified a new mechanism for IFN-α to suppress HCV.
we can now understand the mechanisms by which natural killer cells are able to recognize and kill infected cells, and that we can manipulate this system in order to enhance the immune response.
